topicName: Handling Scope Creep and Mid-Sprint Interruption
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Handling Scope Creep and Mid-Sprint Interruption in Scrum"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scope creep and unexpected mid-sprint interruptions are among the most common threats to Scrum team velocity and morale. When stakeholders introduce new requirements or urgent 'fire drills' occur outside the sprint planning window, the predictability of the sprint goal is immediately compromised."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding the Impact of Interruptions"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Every time a developer is pulled away from their committed sprint backlog items to handle an interruption, context switching occurs. Studies show it can take up to 23 minutes to regain deep focus after a single interruption. Accumulatively, this destroys sprint capacity."},{"order":5,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 1: Enforce the Sprint Goal Boundary"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The Sprint Backlog is locked during Sprint Planning. Changes must go through the Product Owner."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The Sprint Goal acts as a filter. If a new request does not align with the goal, it belongs in the Product Backlog, not the current sprint."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 2: Implement the 1-to-1 Swap Rule (Negotiated Scope)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"If a stakeholder insists that a new, high-priority item must be completed immediately during the current sprint, the Product Owner must negotiate a trade-off. The team cannot simply take on extra work without exceeding capacity."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"New Item Effort == Removed Item Effort (Must match story points)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 3: Handle True Emergencies (The Buffer Approach)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"For teams that regularly face production bugs or urgent support requests, traditional Scrum breaks down unless a buffer is planned. Allocate a specific percentage of capacity (e.g., 15-20%) for unpredicted interruptions, or rotate a 'Buffer Developer' role per sprint."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Step 4: Track Interruption Metrics"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Transparency is key to stopping chronic scope creep. Use your ticketing system (such as Jira) to label mid-sprint additions. During the Sprint Retrospective, review these metrics to show management the true cost of interruptions."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Metric A: Total story points added post-Sprint Planning."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Metric B: Velocity variance caused by unplanned work."},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Protecting the sprint is the shared responsibility of the Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Development Team. By enforcing strict boundaries, utilizing the 1-to-1 swap rule, and maintaining data transparency, teams can maintain high velocity and predictability."}]
